title: EPIC Endgame Analysis!! | Belgrade Gambit | GM Naroditsky’s Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: We face the Nimzowitsch Defence, the knight to c6. In most cases this move has little independent value — meaning it just transposes into another opening.
d4 would give an independent game, but the knight to f3 is easier — Black usually plays e5, and we're back into familiar territory.
I'm in the mood for the Belgrade Gambit — let's see how it holds up at this level.
One downside of committing the knight to f3 is that it rules out the Vienna.
d4 — Black will probably capture. He could also try the old bishop to b4, against which we'd take the knight.
And the Belgrade Gambit — the knight to d5.
The knight to b4 tells me Black knows the theory — it's the recommended, engine-approved move. But I found an interesting weapon that rejuvenates the whole line.
Against the knight to b4, we take on f6. And crucially, against the recapture with the queen, never take on d4 — Qxd4, Qxd4, and the knight forks on c2, winning a piece.
So chase the knight with a3; it has to drop back to c6, its only reasonable square.
A subtle developing move. It may look like there's no way to regain the pawn — and that's true, you're playing this gambit-style; you only win it back if Black commits to d6.
The plan is to meet d6 with the bishop to b5. For now, the flexible bishop to d3 — signalling we're not chasing the pawn back unless Black plays d6.
d6, and now the bishop to b5 — convenient, because it pins the knight, and we're ready to recapture with a small advantage.
Black has a computer line here that holds — very rare for anyone to know it.
The queen takes on d4; the engine wants the bishop to e7 here.
It's not that Black is better — it's just equal. He trades on d4 and we head into an endgame.
I like reaching this endgame — a chance to show how to try to outplay strong players in a long grind.
The endgame should be equal, but White is a touch better for two reasons: slightly better central control, and — more importantly — capturing on c6 will damage Black's queenside pawns.

Take with the knight, not the bishop. The recapture comes with tempo, but I won't hand over the bishop pair or uncontested control of the light squares — taking with the bishop would let Black play c5 and then f5, seizing space.

None of these calls is make-or-break — follow your intuition. The bishop to d3, supporting the e4-pawn, which is a central element of our position; the bishop to a6 did too little after the rook to b8.
Remember: a piece can play a purely defensive role and still be a good piece — don't dismiss this bishop just because it isn't grabbing squares.
The bishop to c4 I avoided because of the bishop to e6 — and we want to dodge trades.
The bishop to e3, eyeing the a7-pawn. We deliberately keep the king's destination open — kingside, queenside, or central, depending on how Black sets up.
There are too many pieces to keep the king in the centre safely — Black would land a rook on e8 and start pressing.

Castle queenside — it tucks the king away, guards b2, and lands the rook on d1, x-raying his bishop. And accept it now: this endgame won't be won quickly. Black is too solid — you improve slowly, one small move at a time, and settle in for a long grind. That's the mindset.
Between b3 and c3: b3 invites a5, then a4 fixes his pawn on a dark square — and creating long-term weaknesses is the whole endgame goal. c3 blunts his bishop; b4 is too committal.
Against my own bullet instinct for c3, I choose b3 — because c3 would leave our b-pawn a long-term weakness and let Black double rooks on the b-file. b3 keeps our queenside healthy.
a4 — fixing his pawn.
Watch for Black's typical break — advancing to c4; if we're forced to take, we get a weakness on a4 and the b-file opens.

I like the bishop to c4 and rook to d3, to smoke his bishop off c3. Not the bishop to d2 — trading dark-squared bishops would make his a5-pawn unattackable, and you never trade away the very piece that attacks a weakness.
There's a tactic behind the rook to d3: if he takes on c4, the rook to c3 skewers his bishop to the c-pawn. The plan is to tie him to the a5 weakness, then open a second front he can't defend.
The rook to d3 — offering him a tactical trap: take on c4, and the rook to c3 wins the c6-pawn.
And the key rule: opposite-coloured bishops are NOT drawish with rooks on the board — no reason to fear that.
Play slowly — the king to b2 for starters.
This gets deeply positional — based on where the pieces belong, not on concrete variations.

I kept f3 in reserve to defend the e4-pawn — that's why I didn't push earlier. His dark-squared bishop is annoying, but c3 would be a bad idea: it softens b3 and kills the bishop-to-d2 plan against a5.
So switch targets — from the a5-pawn to Black's second weakness, the pawn on c6. The idea is the bishop to d2.

The rook to d1, a neutral improving move, also clamping down on the d5-pawn to stop his c5 and e5 breaks. White's better — not by much, a draw with best play — but very unpleasant to defend with all those weaknesses.
The bishop to d2: if he trades, the rook to c3 lands on the prime c5 outpost.
The drawback: he can take and swing a rook to f2 — but it works out concretely. And we keep posing him problems, brutal with his clock low.
The rook to c3 attacks c6, heading for c5, then we double. Not worried about him grabbing e4 — he has three weak pawns to our one, so we come out ahead.
The rook to c5, hitting a5 as well.
The rook to a6 is another slip; the rook to a8 was better. He keeps cooperating with our plan.
Now the principle of more weaknesses — open a second front with exd5.

Break the pawn chain with c4 — it clears the d5-pawn that restricted our rook and opens lines. Now White is much better, maybe technically winning — but rook endgames are treacherous; one slip and he's active.
He's giving up a pawn, sensing the game slip away.
Two ways: the calm rook takes on c6 with check, into a winning three-against-two; or the ambitious rook lift, keeping both rooks on to hit g7.
We take the calmer route — the rook takes on c6 with check.
Now the plan: watch our pieces' activity. Start with the rook to e1 — not the king to c3, which would let his rook infiltrate to e2.
After the rook to e1, the king comes to c3 with a perfect setup — every infiltration square covered.
Phase two: judiciously push the kingside pawns — to create a passer, to restrict his rook, and to soften his structure.
Centralise the rook on e4, preparing b4 for an outside passed pawn.
If we want b4, now is the moment — before he plays c5.
The king to c3 — and if he plays c5, the a5-pawn becomes a long-term weakness we can round up with the rook, or invade on b5 with the king. c5 only weakens him.
A frontal attack on our pawns never succeeds — h5 is met by h4, the rook to g5 by g4.
Lock his pawns up with h4.
Create the passer with b4 — recapture with the king to stay active, close to pushing a5. And on the kingside, gxh4, rook takes h4, and we near a second passer — one on each wing.
Two passed pawns on opposite wings — this has to be winning; now it's a matter of technique.
Cut his king off.
Honestly I feel this has become a draw — I'm being outplayed here.
Still, push f4 — very hard for him to hold.
The automatic c5 actually loses — the rook check on e6, then back to e5.
This is a Lucena position — his king is cut right off, so we simply push the pawn; checks from behind don't matter. Bring the king to f8, push f7, and it's the textbook win.
